appraisal_events.evidence: « Bravo, la vieille ! » s'écriait-il en battant des mains comme au théâtre... Mme d'Arpajon ne fut pas sensible à ce qu'on vantât sa dextérité aux dépens de sa jeunesse.
appraisal_events.explanation: After being drenched by the fountain, Mme d'Arpajon is loudly mocked before the assembled guests by the grand-duc, whose 'consoling' remark is really a jibe at her age; the narrator confirms she felt the insult.

appraisal_events.evidence: l'absence du Prince... grossissait autour de M. de Charlus la foule des invités, de même que, quand Louis XIV n'était pas à Versailles, il y avait plus de monde chez Monsieur, son frère... Bréauté était moins puissant qu'Hubert Robert.
appraisal_events.explanation: With the Prince absent, the crowd gathers around Charlus instead, an effect the narrator compares to the court flocking to the king's brother; Charlus then confirms his commanding wit by dismissing Bréauté's taste and influence as trivial next to the painter Hubert Robert.

status_effects.explanation: She is publicly humiliated and mocked over her age, though she keeps her composure and deflects the aftermath without help.
The narrator frames Charlus, via the Louis XIV analogy, as the true local center of gravity of the gathering in the Prince's absence.
His ironic monologue and dismissal of Bréauté's judgment display commanding wit that the curious, half-indecent crowd defers to.
Charlus publicly belittles Bréauté's taste (the lampions) and declares him 'less powerful' than the artist Hubert Robert.

ambiguities: Charlus's elevation is narrated with a critical edge (his 'impertinence de grand seigneur' and 'égaillement d'hystérique'), so his social and rhetorical dominance is real but shadowed by an unflattering characterization of his manner.
